attacks.claim: Open-data export publishes birth_year, gender, zip, ward, and ranking per poll with verified flag and timestamp, all tied to individual rows; the combination of zip + birth_year + gender + ward + created_at is a quasi-identifier set that can re-identify individual residents, and the data is public CC-BY and irreversible once published. Verified-resident demographics collected for jury-pool balance are being repurposed for public release without stated consent.
attacks.evidence: "one CSV per poll on data.ourtown.org with columns ward, zip, birth_year, gender, ranking, verified, created_at. resident_id is removed before export." ABSENT: k-anonymity or small-cell suppression, aggregation threshold, consent for secondary use of demographic data.

attacks.claim: Voter-file purchase and mass SMS to ~142,000 registered voters is a massive new collection and processing of personal data (mobile numbers from a government file) for a purpose residents never opted into, and it contradicts the stated anonymous-first, optional-verification constraint.
attacks.evidence: "Purchase the county voter registration file from the County Clerk ($400, includes mobile numbers where provided)." / "send an automated SMS to every registered voter in the city (~142,000)" ABSENT: lawful basis, consent, purpose limitation, retention/deletion plan for imported numbers.

attacks.claim: Unsolicited automated SMS to 142,000 people using purchased voter-file numbers with 3 reminders violates the TCPA (prior express consent required for autodialed/marketing-type texts to cell phones), with significant statutory damages per message. Voter-file numbers are not consent. Also the plan treats STOP as sufficient but TCPA requires consent before first send. Election/political-adjacent messaging may trigger additional state rules.
attacks.evidence: "Reply STOP handled by Twilio's default opt-out." ABSENT: documented prior express consent, legal review, carrier 10DLC registration, quiet-hours handling.

attacks.claim: Mass outreach to the entire voter roll is an election-adjacent civic messaging campaign by a nonprofit that may interact with restrictions on government-funded or lobbying/political activity and with public-entity advocacy rules; no legal review is referenced.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: legal/compliance sign-off on council-related civic messaging and nonprofit status constraints.

attacks.claim: Survey data does not support building polls: only 9% of respondents asked for polls, while the top requests (vote visibility, notifications, summaries) are not addressed. The 'centerpiece' framing is contradicted by the plan's own background section.
attacks.evidence: "Polls on upcoming items — 9%" vs "Ward Voice ... is the centerpiece of the FY27 roadmap."

attacks.claim: Success metric of 30% new residents and 6,000 responses is unsupported by any prototype or baseline, and the outreach is the only plausible driver; the metric does not separate SMS-driven responses from organic ones.
attacks.evidence: "6,000 poll responses in the first 30 days." ABSENT: baseline, prototype data, conversion assumption.

attacks.claim: Anonymous responses are protected only by device fingerprint and IP rate limits, which are trivially bypassed (fingerprint spoofing, IP rotation); the 'brigade' guard is weak and unverified responses still count in the 'all responses' column, which feeds the IRV results shown publicly and to council staff.
attacks.evidence: "1 response per poll per device fingerprint" and "unverified responses over 3/min from one IP are queued for review" ABSENT: how queued responses are excluded from tallies, bot/CAPTCHA controls.

attacks.claim: Ward is self-selected for unverified users, so ward-level IRV results are trivially manipulable and presented alongside verified results without weighting; the unverified column can be shown to council staff as resident sentiment.
attacks.evidence: "ward is self-selected for unverified users" ABSENT: validation of ward, any reconciliation with address-derived ward.

attacks.claim: Staff cannot edit or delete responses, and poll options freeze on first response, yet there is no mechanism to remove spam, PII accidentally submitted in free text, or fraudulent responses; combined with public CC-BY export, errors become permanent publications.
attacks.evidence: "Staff cannot edit or delete responses" ABSENT: moderation/redaction path for published data.

attacks.claim: Publishing CSVs to a public CC-BY endpoint and sending SMS to 142,000 people are irreversible actions; no rollback, takedown, or kill switch is described for either, and the launch is scheduled before budget hearings with no staged rollout.
attacks.evidence: "Open-data export (weekly, public, CC-BY)" and "Target launch: before the FY27 budget hearings" ABSENT: rollback plan, staged rollout, takedown procedure.

attacks.claim: Four SMS touches to 142,000 numbers is roughly 568,000 messages; Twilio costs plus the $400 purchase are not budgeted, and no spend cap is stated.
attacks.evidence: "3 automated reminders over 10 days" ABSENT: budget and spend cap for SMS.

attacks.claim: Load target of 5k concurrent is set only in week 5 with no sizing for the SMS-driven spike (142k recipients clicking links within hours), and the IRV tally is computed live per request.
attacks.evidence: "load test (target 5k concurrent)" ABSENT: sizing for 142,000 recipients, caching or precomputation of IRV rounds.

attacks.claim: Weekly export and Monday 07:00 PDF email have no failure alerting or retry described.
attacks.evidence: "emailed Monday 07:00" ABSENT: failure handling and alerting.

attacks.claim: Drag-based ranking is the primary input pattern; tap-to-rank is mentioned but no keyboard or screen-reader requirement is stated beyond a late week-5 pass.
attacks.evidence: "drag or tap-to-rank" ABSENT: keyboard and screen-reader spec for ranking.

attacks.claim: Hard dependency on Twilio for all outreach and on a county clerk data purchase; no exit path for phone data or SMS provider.
attacks.evidence: "Load numbers into Twilio" ABSENT: alternative provider or data portability plan.

attacks.claim: Launch framing solves a staff need (between-session feedback) while the resident-requested features are absent, so the plan may deliver little resident value.
attacks.evidence: "Council staff have also told us they lack a structured way to hear from residents" vs survey priorities.

attacks.claim: Storing demographic fields on residents for jury-pool reports and reusing them in public exports couples two unrelated purposes.
attacks.evidence: "collected at optional verification for the jury-pool-style demographic balance reports"

attacks.claim: Results split into verified and all-responses columns without stated labeling may mislead readers into treating unverified tallies as resident consensus.
attacks.evidence: "split into 'verified' and 'all responses' columns"

attacks.claim: The plan describes an anonymous-first product, but the outreach and export pieces require non-anonymous processing of voter data, contradicting the agreed constraint in the context.
attacks.evidence: "Agreed constraint: the product is anonymous-first" vs "Purchase the county voter registration file"

attacks.claim: The open-data export publishes ward, zip, birth_year, gender, ranking, and verified alongside created_at for every response, on a public CC-BY site. Combined with a small per-poll response count and a per-poll CSV, these quasi-identifiers allow re-identification of individuals and linkage of their civic positions to demographics; the plan does not mention k-anonymity, suppression, or aggregation.
attacks.evidence: "one CSV per poll on data.ourtown.org with columns ward, zip, birth_year, gender, ranking, verified, created_at. resident_id is removed before export."

attacks.claim: Verified residents' address, zip, birth_year, and gender were collected for jury-pool balance reports, and are now being reused and exported publicly per poll. This is a purpose-creep repurposing of personal data with no stated consent for public release.
attacks.evidence: "Verified residents already have address, zip, birth_year, gender (collected at optional verification for the jury-pool-style demographic balance reports)."

attacks.claim: Purchasing the county voter file and sending SMS to ~142,000 people who never opted into OurTown is unsolicited messaging of personal data from a government source obtained for election administration, with no consent basis described; it also contradicts the anonymous-first, optional-verification constraint.
attacks.evidence: "Purchase the county voter registration file from the County Clerk ($400, includes mobile numbers where provided). Load numbers into Twilio and send an automated SMS to every registered voter in the city (~142,000)"

attacks.claim: Bulk automated SMS to non-consenting numbers under the TCPA is high-exposure legal risk (statutory damages per message), and relying on Twilio's default STOP handling does not cure the initial send. Use of voter-file data for commercial or non-election purposes may also be restricted by state law; none of this is addressed.
attacks.evidence: "Reply STOP handled by Twilio's default opt-out."

attacks.claim: Publishing voter-derived mobile numbers' source data and demographic fields may violate state voter-file use restrictions and the purchase terms; the plan does not confirm the County Clerk license permits this use.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: no review of County Clerk data-use terms or state voter-file statute.

attacks.claim: Anonymous-first, unverified responses are accepted with self-selected ward, and abuse controls rely on device fingerprint and IP. These are trivially bypassed, so the 'verified' vs 'all' split is the only integrity signal, yet the verified tally is never shown to be meaningful at this response volume.
attacks.evidence: "Rate limit: 1 response per poll per device fingerprint + 1 per verified resident; unverified responses over 3/min from one IP are queued for review."

attacks.claim: The plan claims ward is 'derived from address' for verified users, but the data model stores ward on unverified responses as self-selected input without validation against any boundary; ward-level IRV results can be skewed by arbitrary input, and the spec doesn't say how invalid ward values are rejected.
attacks.evidence: "ward is self-selected for unverified users and derived from address for verified users."

attacks.claim: Ranked-choice IRV tally rules are unspecified: ties, exhausted ballots, partial rankings, and whether ballots ranking a subset are allowed. Results per ward with small n will be unstable, and the 'split' columns could show contradictory winners.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: IRV tie-break and partial-ballot handling; "Live results page: instant-runoff rounds, split into 'verified' and 'all responses' columns."

attacks.claim: The motivating survey does not support the centerpiece. Polls on upcoming items received 9% of responses, the lowest of four options, yet the plan calls Ward Voice 'the centerpiece of the FY27 roadmap' and sets volume targets without justification.
attacks.evidence: "Polls on upcoming items — 9%" vs "Ward Voice ... is the centerpiece of the FY27 roadmap."

attacks.claim: The 6,000-response target and 30% new-user target are asserted with no baseline, conversion estimate, or prototype, and the SMS campaign is the only mechanism listed to reach new users, so the target depends on an unvalidated and likely unlawful blast.
attacks.evidence: "6,000 poll responses in the first 30 days." / "30% of responses from residents not previously active on OurTown."

attacks.claim: SMS cost math is absent: 142,000 recipients × 4 messages (initial + 3 reminders) is about 568,000 Twilio messages plus carrier fees, far beyond the $400 data purchase, with no budget ceiling or cap.
attacks.evidence: "send an automated SMS to every registered voter in the city (~142,000) ... then 3 automated reminders over 10 days."

attacks.claim: Target of 5k concurrent users is set but the launch-week SMS wave would drive traffic spikes at the same moment; no load assumption links the two, and the weekly export and Monday 07:00 PDF job have no stated capacity limits on self-hosted servers.
attacks.evidence: "load test (target 5k concurrent), launch"

attacks.claim: No failure handling for the Twilio pipeline, bounces, or the Monday PDF/email job; no alerting or retry plan, and a mass send on launch has no rollback or pause.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: retry, pause, monitoring, and alerting for the SMS and scheduled exports.

attacks.claim: Public open-data publication and SMS sends are irreversible: once CSVs are published under CC-BY and messages are delivered, they cannot be retracted. The plan has no gate or dry run before those actions.
attacks.evidence: "Open-data export (weekly, public, CC-BY)" and "send an automated SMS to every registered voter"

attacks.claim: Unverified residents face no clear path to verify, and launch SMS links to a poll with no stated explanation of who sent it or why, which reduces trust.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: SMS copy and sender identification.

attacks.claim: The ranking UI is specified as drag or tap-to-rank, but no keyboard, screen-reader, or motion-free alternative is described, and the accessibility pass is compressed into week 5.
attacks.evidence: "resident ranking UI (mobile-first, drag or tap-to-rank)" / "accessibility pass"

attacks.claim: Staff cannot edit responses and options freeze after the first response, but there is no migration or correction path for mistaken poll options once live.
attacks.evidence: "poll options are frozen once the first response arrives."

attacks.claim: SMS delivery depends on a single vendor (Twilio) with no stated exit path or alternative provider.
attacks.evidence: "Load numbers into Twilio"

attacks.claim: The plan asserts the product is an anonymous-first civic tool, but the outreach section moves to mass unsolicited contact, which contradicts the agreed constraint that participation is voluntary and not built on identity-linked data.
attacks.evidence: "Verification is always optional" vs "send an automated SMS to every registered voter in the city (~142,000)"

attacks.claim: Open-data export publishes ward, zip, birth_year, gender, ranking, verified, created_at per poll as public CC-BY CSV. Combined with verified-resident demographics, small wards/zips and birth_year+gender make individual re-identification and linkage to ballots/addresses plausible; resident_id removal does not stop linkability.
attacks.evidence: "one CSV per poll on data.ourtown.org with columns ward, zip, birth_year, gender, ranking, verified, created_at. resident_id is removed before export."

attacks.claim: Verified residents' address, birth_year and gender were collected for jury-pool demographic reports; the plan repurposes this data for public export and staff email without any stated consent or notice change.
attacks.evidence: "Verified residents already have address, zip, birth_year, gender (collected at optional verification for the jury-pool-style demographic balance reports)."

attacks.claim: Purchasing the county voter file and SMS-blasting ~142,000 registered voters with automated messages and reminders is likely a TCPA/CTIA and state voter-file-use violation: voter files are typically restricted to election/campaign purposes, and automated marketing-style SMS to non-consenting numbers violates TCPA absent prior express consent.
attacks.evidence: "Purchase the county voter registration file from the County Clerk ($400, includes mobile numbers where provided)." / "send an automated SMS to every registered voter in the city (~142,000)"

attacks.claim: Outreach sends SMS to people who never opted in, and relies only on STOP-reply default opt-out, which does not satisfy TCPA prior-express-written-consent requirements for autodialed marketing/informational texts; it also omits any identity/consent disclosure.
attacks.evidence: "Reply STOP handled by Twilio's default opt-out."

attacks.claim: Unverified responses are accepted with self-declared ward and no identity check; device fingerprint and IP rate limits are trivially bypassed, so the integrity controls can be spoofed and the 'verified vs unverified' split is the only defense.
attacks.evidence: "1 response per poll per device fingerprint + 1 per verified resident; unverified responses over 3/min from one IP are queued for review."

attacks.claim: Unverified responses over the IP threshold are 'queued for review' but the plan never says what happens to them in tallies, exports, or the staff PDF, nor who reviews them or on what criteria; results and CSV may silently include or exclude them.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: review process, queue disposition, and whether queued responses appear in the live results, open-data CSV, or staff PDF.

attacks.claim: The plan says 'results are shown per ward' but ward for unverified users is self-selected, so per-ward IRV tallies can be trivially skewed; and the 'verified' column is the only integrity signal yet the 6,000-response target and 30% new-user metric create an incentive to count unverified brigade responses.
attacks.evidence: "ward is self-selected for unverified users and derived from address for verified users."

attacks.claim: The product rationale is contradicted by the artifact's own survey: polls on upcoming items got 9%, the lowest-ranked need, yet the plan declares polls the centerpiece of FY27 and builds the entire 5-week plan around them. No evidence links polls to participation outcomes.
attacks.evidence: "Polls on upcoming items — 9%" vs "is the centerpiece of the FY27 roadmap."

attacks.claim: The top survey needs (see votes and reasons, 61%; notifications for my street, 44%; plain-language summaries, 37%) are absent from the build scope, so the plan solves a problem residents ranked last.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: any vote-tracking, notification, or summary features in sections 2 or 7.

attacks.claim: Council staff's stated gap is structured input between public comment sessions; ranked-choice polls with no reporting on how results affect decisions may not address it.
attacks.evidence: "Council staff have also told us they lack a structured way to hear from residents between public-comment sessions."

attacks.claim: Sending ~142,000 SMS plus 3 reminders (~570k messages) in launch week against a 5k concurrent load target creates burst traffic and Twilio throughput/cost spikes; the load test target does not cover the outreach pipeline or the link-click traffic it generates.
attacks.evidence: "send an automated SMS to every registered voter in the city (~142,000) ... then 3 automated reminders over 10 days" / "load test (target 5k concurrent)"

attacks.claim: SMS cost is unbudgeted: ~142k initial plus reminders, plus per-message Twilio fees, carrier surcharges, and the $400 file; no budget math or cap is given.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: SMS cost estimate, budget cap, or spend limit; only "$400" for the file is stated.

attacks.claim: Weekly open-data export and Monday 07:00 staff PDF/email have no stated failure handling, retries, or alerting; a failed export silently leaves public data stale while CC-BY claims remain.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: retry, alerting, or failure-mode handling for the weekly export and Monday email.

attacks.claim: Publishing per-poll CSVs under CC-BY on a public site is irreversible once downloaded; no takedown, redaction, or retraction path is defined for published rows.
attacks.evidence: "Open-data export (weekly, public, CC-BY)" / ABSENT: takedown or retraction process.

attacks.claim: Staff cannot edit or delete responses and options freeze on first response, so a mistaken poll option or erroneous/abusive response cannot be corrected, and the SMS blast cannot be recalled.
attacks.evidence: "Staff cannot edit or delete responses; poll options are frozen once the first response arrives."

attacks.claim: The ranking UI is drag-or-tap and mobile-first with accessibility only a one-week pass in week 5; keyboard and screen-reader ranking support is unspecified and risky to retrofit.
attacks.evidence: "Week 2: resident ranking UI (mobile-first, drag or tap-to-rank)." / "Week 5: accessibility pass"

attacks.claim: Results split into verified and all-responses columns for IRV rounds may confuse residents about which tally is authoritative; no copy or display spec is given.
attacks.evidence: "split into 'verified' and 'all responses' columns."

attacks.claim: SMS pipeline depends on Twilio and the voter file on a county vendor; no exit or self-hosting path is stated for the messaging component.
attacks.evidence: "Load numbers into Twilio"

attacks.claim: Open-data export, staff PDF, and SMS pipeline all land in week 4 with a 3-person team; scope is too large for the schedule and the test plan is absent.
attacks.evidence: "Week 4: open-data export, staff PDF, voter-file import + SMS pipeline."

attacks.claim: Anonymous-first constraint is contradicted by the design: verified-resident demographic fields are exported publicly and the outreach requires a purchased identity-linked voter file, undermining the agreed constraint that verification is optional and identity not required.
attacks.evidence: "residents can participate without verifying identity" vs "Purchase the county voter registration file ... includes mobile numbers"
